name: South Ridge (Bullseye Traverse variant)

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 1 of 3 on a 40 m rope through the technical section.
hazards: The compact granite has few holds and is harder to reverse than to climb; one party found a heather-camouflaged hole in the rock.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 2 of 3 on a 40 m rope through the technical section.
rappel_detail.station: The next anchor down the technical section.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 3 of 3 on a 40 m rope through the technical section, to easier ground. Then reverse the Class 3 traverse to Bullseye Pass.
rappel_detail.station: The next anchor down the technical section.

rappels: 3 rappels on a 40m rope through the technical section
descent_text: From the summit, three rappels on a ~40m rope are needed to get back down through the technical section to easier ground; the granite here is compact with few holds and was reported as harder to reverse than to climb — one party found a heather-camouflaged hole in the rock during the down-climb. Below the rappels, reverse the Class 3 traverse back around the peak to Bullseye Pass.
approach: Reached via the Chain Lakes/Doelle Lakes basin as part of a multi-day traverse (e.g. the 'Bullseye Traverse'), continuing cross-country south to Bullseye Pass (~6,200 ft) before dropping packs and climbing the south side of the peak. No standalone trailhead-to-base mileage for this specific line is documented; it is climbed as a side trip from a traverse camp.
overview: A harder, more direct line up Bulls Tooth's south ridge from Bullseye Pass, done by parties on the multi-summit 'Bullseye Traverse'; unlike the standard notch scramble, this line finishes with a short, roped Class 4-5 pitch to the true summit.
beta: From Bullseye Pass (~6,200 ft), parties drop packs and climb the steep southeast slope on foot/hands to grippy granite, working up and over a hump before dropping beneath the summit on its western side (Class 3 traverse). The final approach to the true summit follows the south ridge and requires roped Class 4-5.0 climbing — two independent accounts describe one to two short pitches on excellent, hold-covered granite, finishing with an exposed high step onto a one-person summit perch.
gear: Small rack of slings/runners (small cams/nuts recommended)
